historical_timeline.summary: Born near Mayesville, South Carolina, to formerly enslaved parents.
Marries Albertus Bethune after her schooling.
Founds her school for girls in Daytona Beach.
Founds the National Council of Negro Women; leads Negro affairs at the National Youth Administration.
After a severe asthma attack, gives up the college presidency.
Asthma attacks recur in her correspondence; the Council House is bought in Washington.
Leaves public life at 75 for her home on the campus.
Dies of a heart attack in Daytona Beach at 79.

claims.statement: Mary Jane McLeod was born on July 10, 1875, near Mayesville, South Carolina, the fifteenth of seventeen children of Samuel and Patsy McLeod. Her parents, and eight of her older siblings, had been enslaved; after emancipation the family bought five acres of land and farmed cotton.

claims.statement: She was the only McLeod child to get an education, first at a Presbyterian mission school near Mayesville and then at Scotia Seminary. In 1898 she married Albertus Bethune; they separated after about nine years without divorcing, and he died in 1918.

claims.statement: In 1904 she founded a school for Black girls in Daytona Beach, Florida. She opened McLeod Hospital there in 1911, which the National Park Service says played a critical role in containing the influenza pandemic of 1918, and she and her students faced down the Ku Klux Klan at the school. The school merged with the Cookman Institute (dated 1923 by the National Park Service; named Bethune-Cookman College in 1929 according to another reference), and she was its president until 1942.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her documented life's work as an educator anchors the modern social history.

claims.statement: She was president of the National Association of Colored Women from 1924, received the NAACP's Spingarn Medal in 1935, and founded the National Council of Negro Women on December 5, 1935. She directed the Division of Negro Affairs of the National Youth Administration from the mid-1930s until it closed in 1943 and led the informal group of Black federal advisers known as the Black Cabinet. She said of her place in Washington: "When they see me, they know that the Negro is present."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her documented national leadership and constant travel anchor the modern social history and her concern about being able to keep working.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Confirm asthma in a 72-year-old Black woman with years of wheeze and breathlessness who has been treated with albuterol alone, and tell it apart from COPD and heart failure: spirometry with bronchodilator response interpreted with race-neutral equations, DLCO, FeNO and blood eosinophils, chest X-ray, BNP and echocardiography. Then treat on GINA 2025 track 1 (budesonide-formoterol as maintenance and reliever, with SABA-only treatment stopped) and the 2020 NAEPP focused update, check inhaler technique and adherence before any step-up, write an asthma action plan, manage an exacerbation and review after it, assess for biologic therapy against the definition of severe asthma, and treat the comorbidities that worsen asthma (chronic rhinosinusitis, reflux, obesity without stigma) and the hypertensive heart disease found on the echocardiogram, with vaccinations; Black Americans have higher asthma death rates and race-based spirometry equations have hidden lung impairment, so each step is checked for under-treatment.

visit_schedule.purpose: New patient visit for four months of wheeze, night cough and breathlessness on exertion in a 72-year-old woman with long-standing asthma that was never confirmed: examination, chest X-ray, ECG, blood tests and BNP, and planning of lung function testing and an echocardiogram

Diagnosis visit: spirometry, FeNO and echocardiogram results with the pulmonology consultation; asthma confirmed, heart failure excluded, hypertensive heart disease found; start of budesonide-formoterol as maintenance and reliever
Six-week asthma review: control, inhaler technique and adherence, the ear, nose and throat result, blood pressure and reflux
Same-day sick visit for an asthma exacerbation with a cold
Review six weeks after an exacerbation: control, repeat spirometry and FeNO, biologic assessment, blood pressure and the post-exacerbation plan

consultant_note.history: Mrs. Bethune, 72, is seen at the request of Dr. Harrington-Mbeki for four months of worsening wheeze, night cough and breathlessness on exertion, on a background of asthma diagnosed clinically many years ago and never confirmed. She uses albuterol most days and has never had an inhaled corticosteroid. Triggers are colds, dust, perfume and humid air. She has never smoked. She has nasal blockage, postnasal drip and reduced smell, and evening heartburn. She has had no oral corticosteroid course, emergency visit or admission for asthma in the past year
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Harrington-Mbeki's intake note and results: chest X-ray with mild hyperinflation and normal heart size; ECG with LVH by voltage; blood eosinophils 0.42; BNP 48; Asthma Control Test 13. This morning, in our laboratory, with GLI Global race-neutral equations: FEV1 1.30 L (64 percent predicted) before and 1.57 L after albuterol 400 mcg (+270 mL, +21 percent); FEV1/FVC 0.64 before and 0.72 after; DLCO 17.2 (92 percent predicted); FeNO 46 ppb. Total IgE 210 IU/mL; specific IgE positive to house dust mite, negative to cat, dog, cockroach and mold. Transthoracic echocardiogram this morning: ejection fraction 62 percent, mild concentric LVH, grade 1 diastolic dysfunction, normal left atrium and right ventricle, estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 28 mmHg

assessment.display: Asthma, confirmed, uncontrolled, with type 2 inflammation
assessment.assessment: Question 1: this is asthma. The 270 mL, 21 percent bronchodilator response confirms variable airflow obstruction, and the post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC of 0.72 with a normal DLCO argues against COPD, which in any case would be unusual in a never smoker. Question 2: read with race-neutral GLI Global equations, as the American Thoracic Society now recommends, her FEV1 is 64 percent of predicted; race-based equations would have set a lower predicted value for her and made the impairment look milder, which is one way asthma in Black patients has been under-recognized. Question 4: FeNO 46 ppb, eosinophils 0.42, total IgE 210 and dust mite sensitization show type 2 (allergic and eosinophilic) inflammation. She does not have severe asthma, because she has never been treated with an inhaled corticosteroid, so biologic therapy is not indicated now; if she remained uncontrolled on optimized step 4 to 5 treatment, or had repeated oral corticosteroid courses, she would qualify for assessment, and anti-IL-5 or anti-IL-4 receptor therapy would fit her phenotype

assessment.display: Hypertensive heart disease without heart failure
assessment.assessment: Question 1, continued: her breathlessness is not cardiac. BNP is 48, the ejection fraction is normal, the left atrium is not enlarged and there is no pulmonary hypertension. The LVH and grade 1 diastolic dysfunction reflect untreated hypertension, which should be treated; a beta-blocker should be avoided

Question 5: probable chronic rhinosinusitis, which worsens asthma control; nasal endoscopy will confirm it and look for polyps, which would also matter for any later biologic choice. Reflux should be treated for its own symptoms; obesity can add to breathlessness, but here asthma is the main cause

recommendations: Question 3: stop albuterol alone and start GINA track 1 budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg as maintenance and reliever: one inhalation twice daily and one as needed, up to 12 a day (step 3)
Check inhaler technique and adherence at every visit and correct them before any step-up; add a spacer if the technique with the pressurized inhaler is poor

Question 6: a written asthma action plan with peak flow zones, a peak flow meter and a diary to set her personal best; review six weeks after starting and within a week of any exacerbation; Asthma Control Test at each visit; repeat spirometry and FeNO after three to six months
Treat the upper airway: intranasal fluticasone and saline now, and ear, nose and throat review with nasal endoscopy
Treat symptomatic reflux with an eight-week course of a proton pump inhibitor and meal timing; it is not a treatment for asthma
Hypertension: amlodipine or another agent without beta-blockade; avoid nonselective beta-blockers, including eye drops
Biologic therapy is not indicated now; repeat blood eosinophils and reassess if asthma is uncontrolled on step 4 to 5 treatment or she needs two or more oral corticosteroid courses in a year
Vaccines: pneumococcal vaccine now; influenza, COVID-19 and RSV in the autumn; house dust mite covers for the bedding
